report:
## Conclusion

Yes — for people at high risk of lung cancer (chiefly heavy current or former smokers), regular low-dose CT (LDCT) screening reduces lung cancer mortality, based on strong randomized-trial evidence.

**Key evidence**

- The U.S. **National Lung Screening Trial (NLST)**, which enrolled 53,454 current/former heavy smokers (≥30 pack-years, ages 55–74), found a **20% relative reduction in lung cancer mortality** and a 6.7% reduction in all-cause mortality with three annual LDCT screens versus chest X-ray (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873; https://www.cancer.gov/types/lung/research/nlst).
- The European **NELSON trial**, involving >15,000 high-risk men and women screened at years 1, 3, 5.5, and 8, showed a **24% mortality reduction in men and up to 33% in women** after 10 years, confirming and even exceeding NLST's benefit (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanres/article/PIIS2213-2600(20)30059-X/fulltext; https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793).
- A pooled meta-analysis of nine randomized trials found an overall **16% reduction in lung cancer mortality** (relative rate ~0.84), reinforcing consistency across trials, though not every individual smaller trial (e.g., some European studies) reached statistical significance alone (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0959804925003521).

**Caveats:** Benefits are concentrated in truly high-risk populations (heavy smoking history, older age); screening carries real harms including high false-positive rates (up to ~13%), overdiagnosis, incidental findings, and radiation exposure, and it does not reduce smoking-cessation-independent risk (https://publications.ersnet.org/content/errev/33/172/230232). Overall, major guidelines (USPSTF, NCI) now recommend annual LDCT for eligible heavy smokers, given the net mortality benefit demonstrated across trials.
